title: More Children Face Deportation in New Jersey as Justice Department Accelerates Immigration Backlog Push
excerpt: Legal advocates say Newark's immigration court is lumping children into adult hearings with as many as 50 immigrants per session, rescheduling cases from 2028 to 2026.
body:
• Children and young adults in New Jersey face sharply higher deportation risk as the Justice Department prioritises reducing the immigration court backlog under the Trump administration's mass deportation agenda.
  • Legal advocates report that Newark's immigration court is scheduling hearings with up to 50 immigrants at once, lumping children into adult proceedings and rescheduling cases from 2028 to 2026.
  • A ProPublica analysis found unaccompanied minors are being detained and removed at three times the rate of Trump's first term.
  • Across the country, legal aid organisations face a funding crisis after the federal government withheld $65 million in fees for counsel already provided to migrant children.

Mass Hearings in Newark

The federal immigration court in Newark, New Jersey, has become ground zero for the Trump administration's push to clear a massive case backlog — and children are being swept up in the process.

https://x.com/northjersey/status/2081718786143436965

Local legal advocacy groups say that over the past three months, the court has undergone a dramatic shift. Hearings now routinely summon as many as 50 immigrants at a time. Cases previously scheduled for 2028 are being pulled forward to 2026. And in what attorneys describe as an alarming departure from past practice, children are being grouped into adult hearings rather than receiving separate proceedings.

"It feels like Newark is the new Texas," said Priscilla Monico Marín, executive director of the New Jersey Consortium for Immigrant Children, which provides legal representation for undocumented children.

"You have this disturbing trend of many, many kids being ordered removed from the United States. In the last few months, we are seeing kids on a waitlist for an attorney with possible relief that are being ordered removed."

— Priscilla Monico Marín, NJ Consortium for Immigrant Children

The Justice Department's Position

The Justice Department makes no apology for the pace. "Reducing the immigration court backlog remains one of the highest priorities for this administration," a spokesperson said. "The Justice Department is restoring integrity to our immigration system by hearing cases fairly, expeditiously and uniformly, in accordance with the law."

The backlog is enormous — millions of cases accumulated over years. But critics argue that speed is coming at the cost of due process, particularly for the most vulnerable respondents in the system.

Children Removed at Triple the Rate

The pressure on Newark is part of a nationwide pattern. A ProPublica analysis published on July 6 found that unaccompanied minors are being detained and removed from the country at three times the rate seen during the final years of Trump's first term.

In Oregon, hundreds of unaccompanied children face the prospect of losing legal counsel entirely. Advocacy organisations report that the federal government has conditioned reimbursement of $65 million in fees — for counsel already provided — on organisations handing over attorney-client privileged information about their young clients. Most have refused.

"This administration is attempting to starve the immigration legal system into submission," said Frank Garcia, executive director of Immigration Counseling Services in Oregon, which has $560,000 in outstanding reimbursements and may need to downsize or close by November if funding does not improve.

A Broader Enforcement Push

The acceleration in court proceedings comes alongside expanded enforcement on the ground. In New Jersey, the Department of Homeland Security continues community-level immigration enforcement through ICE officers and has revived a proposal to convert a warehouse in Roxbury Township, Morris County, into an immigrant detention centre.

Meanwhile, the Board of Immigration Appeals has issued decisions limiting continuances — the delays that give respondents time to find lawyers or gather evidence — and restricting the administrative closure of cases, a tool judges previously used to manage their dockets.

What It Means for Immigrant Families

For the Indian diaspora, many of whom have family members navigating the immigration system through asylum claims, green card backlogs, or adjustment of status proceedings, the changes signal a fundamentally different courtroom environment. Cases that once had years of lead time are being called up in months. And for children in the system without legal representation, the consequences of a missed hearing or an unprepared case are no longer theoretical — they are immediate.
